hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you hope the people you love will still carry after you?
options: then you’ll understand this old man. listen.
then this story might start you thinking. listen.
that’s honest. listen anyway, this one is gentle.

steps.line: The Talmud tells this story. Jacob, the man renamed Israel, was very old, near the end of his life in Egypt. His twelve sons gathered around his bed.
He had one fear. Would his children keep his faith after he was gone? Maybe one of them didn’t believe what he believed.
His sons answered together: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. Just as there is only One in your heart, so in ours.”

steps.q: In a Torah scroll, two letters of the Shema are written extra large. Together they spell a word. Which?
steps.why: The big ayin and dalet spell ed, witness. Saying the Shema, many teachers say, you testify, the way the sons did for their father.

steps.q: The sons have answered. How do you think Jacob responds?
o: He asks each son to swear an oath
He answers with a blessing of his own
He says nothing, and closes his eyes
steps.why: He answers with a blessing, softly. Many Jews still say his line in a whisper.

steps.line: And Jacob, at peace, answered softly: “Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever.”

steps.q: Why is it so moving that the sons say “Hear, O Israel” to their father?
o: Israel was their father’s own new name
Israel was the name of the oldest son
Israel was the land they were living in
steps.why: Israel was Jacob’s name, from the night he wrestled. His sons spoke his name back to him, with his faith inside it.

steps.line: Today, those six words, Shema Yisrael, are said morning and night. Many cover their eyes with one hand, to shut everything else out and just listen.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Why do many say Jacob’s line, “Blessed be the name…,” in a whisper?
o: Jacob was too weak to speak aloud
To keep it hidden from enemies
It isn’t in the Torah, so it’s said softly
steps.why: Pesachim 56a: Jacob said it, but Moses didn’t write it in the Torah. So the rabbis split the difference: say it, softly. On Yom Kippur it’s said aloud.

steps.line: Some children learn it as their first prayer, at bedtime. And tradition hopes it will be among the last words a person says, just like at Jacob’s bed.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. the shema isn’t said to god. it’s said to israel: to the people, to yourself. it’s a wake-up call.
and in hebrew, shema means more than hearing with your ears. it means listen, pay attention, take it to heart. said at the start of the day and the end, and of a life.

steps.q: The Talmud says Rabbi Akiva died a martyr saying the Shema, holding one word until his last breath. Which word?
steps.why: His soul left him on echad (Berakhot 61b). That’s why many hope the Shema is among their last words, as it was at Jacob’s bed.

today.say: tonight, before you sleep, try covering your eyes for a few seconds and just listen. you can say the six words, or simply listen. watch, learn or join in, it’s your choice.
options: a hand over your eyes. that’s how it begins.
that’s the heart of it. shema means listen.
